blocks.prompt: Gold, Silver, and Bronze
blocks.text: A medal is a small metal award you can wear on a ribbon. People win medals for winning races, for being brave, or for doing something no one has done before. At the Olympic Games, the top three athletes in each event win medals. First place wins gold, second place wins silver, and third place wins bronze. This order did not always exist. At the 1904 Olympic Games in St. Louis, medals were handed out in gold, silver, and bronze for the first time. The idea stuck, and today almost every sport copies it. Here is something surprising. An Olympic gold medal is not solid gold. It is mostly silver with a thin layer of real gold on the outside. Solid gold would cost far too much and would be very heavy. Bronze is a mix of two metals, copper and tin, which people have used for thousands of years. A medal is really a way to freeze one moment in metal, so the person who earned it can hold that day again and again.

blocks.prompt: What a Medal Is Really Made Of
blocks.text: For as long as people have competed, they have wanted proof that they won. The ancient Greeks held their own Olympic Games more than two thousand years ago, but the champions did not receive medals. They were crowned with a wreath of wild olive leaves. The leaves dried and crumbled, but the honor lasted a lifetime. Metal medals as sport prizes are a much newer idea. When the modern Olympic Games began in 1896, the winner received a silver medal, not a gold one. Gold, silver, and bronze for the top three became the rule at the 1904 Games in St. Louis, and the world has followed it ever since. Look closely at an Olympic gold medal and you will find a surprise. It is not solid gold. The rules only require a thin coating of real gold, at least six grams, over a medal that is mostly silver. Solid gold would be enormously expensive and heavy enough to be uncomfortable to wear. Bronze, the third place metal, is one of the oldest human inventions: copper mixed with tin, first made thousands of years ago. Medals hang from ribbons for a simple reason. A ribbon lets the winner wear the award around the neck, where everyone can see it, and where the athlete can feel its weight. Some medals now carry a modern twist. The medals for the Tokyo Games were made from metal taken out of millions of old phones and other electronics that people donated. A medal, in the end, is a memory you can hold, shaped out of metal so the moment does not fade.

blocks.prompt: The Story Hidden in a Medal
blocks.text: A medal is one of the smallest objects a person can win and one of the heaviest to carry. It weighs only a few hundred grams, yet athletes train for a decade to feel that weight around their neck. To understand why a disc of metal matters so much, it helps to look at where medals come from and what they are actually made of. The ancient Greeks, who invented the Olympic Games, did not award medals at all. Their champions received a kotinos, a wreath cut from a sacred wild olive tree. The wreath was worth nothing as material, and that was the point: the honor lived in the winning, not in the prize. Metal awards for athletes arrived much later. At the first modern Olympics in 1896, the champion of each event was given a silver medal and an olive branch, while the runner-up received bronze. The now familiar ranking of gold, silver, and bronze for the top three was not fixed until the 1904 Games in St. Louis. Once it appeared, it spread to nearly every sport on Earth. The metals themselves tell a story about value. Gold has always been rare, soft, and bright, which is why cultures across history have tied it to first place and highest worth. Yet an Olympic gold medal is a small deception. It is not solid gold. Olympic rules demand only that it be plated with at least six grams of real gold over a body that is mostly silver. A solid gold medal would cost a fortune and hang heavily enough to be a burden. Silver takes second, and bronze, an ancient blend of copper and tin, takes third. The order mirrors how humans learned to work these metals and how rare each one is. What a medal really does is turn a moment into an object. A race lasts seconds and then it is gone, but the medal remains. The winner can hold it, show it, and pass it to their children long after the crowd has left. That is why organizers keep finding new meaning to pour into them. The medals for the Tokyo Games were forged from gold, silver, and bronze pulled out of millions of discarded phones and gadgets, turning electronic trash into the highest honor in sport. The medal proves that the smallest prize can carry the largest memory.

blocks.prompt: Forged from Trash and Triumph: The Truth About the Medal
blocks.text: Few objects carry as much weight for their size as a medal. A gold medal from the modern Olympic Games weighs only around half a kilogram, yet athletes will surrender years of ordinary life to earn one. That gap, between what a medal is and what it means, is the whole mystery of the thing, and it is older than any stadium. The people who invented the Olympic Games did not use medals. When athletes competed at Olympia more than two and a half thousand years ago, the single champion of each event was crowned with a kotinos, a wreath of wild olive cut from a sacred grove. There was no second place and no third. The wreath was worthless as material and priceless as honor, and the ancient Greeks preferred it that way, because a prize with no cash value could only be won, never bought. Metal awards for sport are a modern invention. At the first modern Olympics, held in Athens in 1896, the victor of each event received a silver medal, and the runner-up received bronze. Gold did not yet sit at the top. The ranking the world now takes for granted, gold for first, silver for second, bronze for third, was not standardized until the 1904 Games in St. Louis. From there it spread until almost every competition on the planet borrowed it. The metals were not chosen at random. They follow the order in which humans learned to work them and the rarity of each in the ground. Bronze, a blend of copper and tin, was the first alloy people ever made, and it named an entire age of history. Silver is rarer and brighter. Gold is rarest of all, and so soft and so resistant to tarnish that nearly every culture has linked it to permanence and to first place. Yet the Olympic gold medal hides a quiet contradiction. It is not made of gold. Olympic rules require only that a gold medal be plated with a minimum of six grams of the metal over a core that is at least ninety-two percent silver. A solid gold medal would be ruinously expensive and heavy enough to strain the neck that wore it. The grandest prize in sport is, in truth, a silver medal wearing a thin gold coat. None of this diminishes the medal, because a medal was never really about its metal. Its true function is to freeze a moment. A race is over in seconds and a career in a few short years, but the object endures. It can be held, displayed, and handed down long after the roar of the crowd has faded. Understanding this, the organizers of recent Games have begun to load medals with extra meaning. Every medal awarded at the Tokyo Games was forged from gold, silver, and bronze extracted from roughly six million discarded phones and electronic devices, donated by the public and melted down. The highest honor in sport was literally reclaimed from the trash. A medal, then, is a small paradox you can hold in your palm: a cheap thing made precious, a passing moment made to last, proof that value lives not in what an object is made of, but in what it is made to mean.
